tagline.text: A volcanic island beside Leyte, packed with waterfalls and hidden islets

location.label: Location
location.text: Biliran Province (8 municipalities including Naval, Almeria and Caibiran)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000–6,000 (per person, 2 nights 3 days, including lodging, transport and fees)

children.text: Biliran is a mountainous island just north of Leyte, with waterfalls, multi-tiered gorges, sulfur vents and small outlying islands. A bridge connects it to Leyte by land, so you can plan anything from a day trip to a multi-day stay from Tacloban or Ormoc.

Biliran is the island that makes up Biliran Province in the Eastern Visayas region of the Philippines. It lies north of Leyte, and the Biliran Strait between them is less than 1 km wide. The province covers about
536 km²

and became a province in its own right, separate from Leyte, on May 11, 1992 under Republic Act 7160. The capital, Naval, sits on the west coast and is also the largest town. The island holds 8 municipalities, and Maripipi Island to the northwest also belongs to the province.

The terrain is mostly mountainous, with only narrow flatlands along the coast and wider plains around Naval and Caibiran. The highest point is around 1,300 m above sea level, though sources differ slightly on the peak's name (Mount Naliwatan or Mount Suiro) and its height. The island has five active sulfur vent (solfatara) areas, and the only recorded eruption was a steam eruption on September 26, 1939. This terrain means plenty of water, which explains the many waterfalls, and there is also geothermal energy potential.

Biliran's appeal is not beach resorts but hands-on nature: swimming in cool waterfalls, canyoning down a river gorge, bat caves, rice terraces and hopping to small islands by boat. It is not yet a package-tour destination, so crowds are small and prices are low, but that also means little signage and slow travel. The waterfalls are scattered across three areas (Almeria, Caibiran and Cabucgayan), so it works best to cover one area per day.

This entry covers Biliran Island as a whole. Places with their own entries, such as Sambawan Island, are linked under Nearby. Transport schedules and fares change from year to year, so please check the latest information before you go.
This waterfall in Almeria is about
(roughly 100 ft) high, and you walk about
30 minutes

from the drop-off point where the motorcycle taxi leaves you. The water is clear and cold, which is welcome in the midday heat, but one travel blogger wrote that the current was strong during the visit, so they stayed on the rocks and only dipped briefly in a shallow pool. Water volume and clarity change after rain, so ask locals about conditions before getting in.

Kasabangan Falls is in Cabucgayan and is known as a 13-tier waterfall. Some say it is among the smaller falls in Biliran, but it sits high in the mountains, so the climb itself is the adventure. Rather than trying to reach the top in one go, decide how many tiers you can handle, and bring grippy shoes and a local guide so you do not slip on wet rock.
Recoletos Falls lies just above Ulan-Ulan Falls and, depending on the source, is about
high. It has a deep green pool that is good for swimming, and some visitors jump in from a tree branch. Nearby Bagongbong Falls (about
9 m
) is easy to skip if your guide does not know the way, so confirm that before you set out. It is common to string several falls together in one day by motorcycle taxi (habal-habal).

blocks.title: Sambawan Island and Tingkasan Bat Cave

children.text: Tingkasan Bat Cave is a stop on the way to Sambawan Island. The cave is dark and the floor can be slippery, so you need a headlamp and a local guide. Sambawan Island is covered in its own entry.

These rice terraces are in Almeria. The view is best just before planting or when the rice is green. They are smaller than the vast terraces of northern Luzon, but you will have them almost to yourself.
The Sampao River in Almeria is a venue for adventure canyoning, with jumps and rappels as you work your way downstream. Always book a local guide and an operator with proper safety gear.

blocks.title: Panamao Museum and the outlying islands

children.text: The Panamao Museum inside the Provincial Capitol is free to enter and is a good quick introduction to Biliran's history and daily life. It is said to be open

, which suits a short visit on the day you arrive by boat or plane. Outlying islands such as Higatangan (reachable from Naval by pump boat, a small motorboat), Dalutan, Capiñahan and Maripipi also exist, so ask at Naval port or your lodging about boats.

blocks.title: Tinago Falls and the big falls of Caibiran

children.text: Tinago Falls in Caibiran is about

(90 ft) high and sits inside Tinago Eco-Tourism Park, which has an amphitheater, picnic areas, restrooms and shower rooms. The main pool has a strong current and large boulders, so swimming there is reported to be risky. Casiawan Falls in Cabucgayan is about
(130 ft) and is said to be the highest in the province, and Tomalistis Falls in Caibiran is described as having sweet-tasting water that earned a Guinness mention. Some falls reportedly charge around
per person, but this varies from fall to fall, so check on site.

Drop your bags at your lodging, visit the Panamao Museum, then get cash from an ATM and stock up on snacks in Naval town.
Hire a habal-habal for the day and head to the falls toward Almeria (Ulan-Ulan and Bagongbong). Negotiate the fare in advance.
See the Iyusan Rice Terraces and return to Naval before sunset.
Depending on boat times, take a ferry from Naval port to Cebu or travel back to Tacloban.
Rain is frequent in Biliran, so leaving one spare day in your schedule gives you a backup if the waterfall plans are canceled.

Tour the Almeria area on the waterfall route.
Go to Sambawan Island via Tingkasan Bat Cave. Boats depend heavily on the weather, so confirm locally before booking.
Return to Naval and continue your journey.
Several direct flights a day run from Manila (NAIA) to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport, Tacloban (TAC).
A shuttle connects the airport to the Tacloban bus terminal.

Biliran Airport in Naval has a 1,000 m runway, but you need to confirm locally whether any commercial service runs.
Several bus companies run direct from Manila to Naval. It is a long-distance route that crosses Leyte by ferry, so it takes a long time.
Confirm arrival times and fares at the terminal before boarding.

Habal-habal (motorcycle taxis) are the most common transport and can be hired for the day. Expect to negotiate.

Within Naval, use tricycles and habal-habal.
Biliran has no clear dry season. Average annual rainfall is about 2,555 mm, with rain on around 200 days a year, and December is the wettest month. Average temperatures are generally

If waterfalls and island hopping are your goal, spring, when rain is relatively lighter, is recommended. In wetter months the falls run strong, but trails are slippery and some days boats cannot sail.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Waterfalls are full, but boat and mountain plans are easily canceled.
The most reliable time for waterfalls and island hopping.
Check typhoon news and ferry cancellations, and leave plenty of slack in your schedule.

Most lodging is in Naval. Older listings mention basic rooms from ₱300, air-conditioned rooms in the ₱500–800 range, places with swimming pools, and garden resorts from about ₱1,300. Prices come from old data, so confirm them before booking. There are also seaside options, such as Agta Beach Resort in Almeria.

Naval has 24-hour ATMs (Metrobank and PNB) and supermarkets. Before heading out to the falls or islands, stock up on cash, bottled water and snacks. Restaurants focus on fish, seafood and local rice-meal eateries, and outlying sights have almost no restaurants, so packing a lunch is safest. For waterfall days it is convenient to hire a habal-habal for the day. A 2020 traveler's report put a day hire for two people at about
, but this varies with distance and negotiation, so agree on the price before you leave.
Hiring a habal-habal for the day is the easiest way to reach waterfall trailheads. Agree on the price and the return time before you set off.
Bring sandals that can get wet, a waterproof bag and a towel. Wet rocks are very slippery.
Boats (to Cebu and for island hopping) are canceled in bad weather. Leave slack on your last day.
ATMs are in Naval town. Cards do not work at rural waterfalls or on the islands, so bring plenty of cash.
Visiting caves requires a headlamp and a local guide.
Sambawan Island has its own entry, so decide first whether to include it in your plan.
Entrance and guide fees differ from fall to fall and are often cash only, so carry plenty of small bills.
At the falls in Almeria, do not leave belongings unattended, and leave valuables at your lodging.
Biliran has active sulfur vents and heavy rain, so landslides and flash floods in gorges are real risks. Do not enter gorges or waterfalls on rainy days.
Waterfalls and canyoning can swell suddenly after rain. Follow your local guide's judgment.
Mobile signal is weak in some outlying areas. Do not hike mountain trails alone, and avoid swimming where the current is strong in waterfall pools.
During typhoon season, ferries and boats stop running, so check the latest weather and service notices.
Near the sulfur vents, toxic gas and hot ground can be present, so do not approach without a guide.
The best-known outlying island reached by boat from Biliran. Boats vary with the weather, so confirm locally.
